summary: Gives guidelines for using XML in IETF protocols. XML has become a widely used way of representing structured data, and many protocols need such a representation. This Best Current Practice discusses when XML is appropriate and what to consider when designing with it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3470 gives IETF protocol designers guidance for using XML to represent structured data. It does not say that protocols should choose XML; it explains the decisions to make if they do.

questions: when to use xml in a protocol
when should a protocol use xml
which media type should xml protocols use
subtitle: Design guidance for using XML to represent structured data in IETF protocols.

tldr.problem: Protocol designers need to represent structured data, and XML offers readable, extensible text but also adds processing, size, and security considerations.
tldr.mechanism: This Best Current Practice compares XML with other formats and recommends how protocol specifications should handle syntax, extensions, namespaces, character encoding, media types, and security.
tldr.outcome: The guidance became BCP 70 and applies when a protocol chooses XML. RFC 8996 later updates this document.

today: RFC 3470 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 70), published in January 2003. The unit metadata says it has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Scope of the Guidelines
sections.content:
XML is a framework for structuring data and is used to represent data in protocol exchanges. This document guides designers who include XML within a larger Internet protocol and sets IETF policy for standards-track protocol documents.

The document does not promote XML as the preferred representation. It excludes ordinary email or web delivery of XML, protocols built entirely around XML, and higher-level XML representation frameworks.
sections.plainLanguage: This guidance applies when a protocol uses XML as one part of its data exchange. It leaves the choice of format to protocol designers.

sections.title: Choosing XML or Another Format
sections.content:
XML offers built-in framing, human-readable text, support for international characters, and extensibility. Common tools can create and inspect XML, and formal definitions can constrain its structure.

XML can be verbose and slower to process than compact representations. It has no native detailed data typing, and binary data must be encoded as text. For fundamental protocols with high performance requirements and modest extensibility needs, the RFC says fixed binary data may be more appropriate. It compares XML with ASN.1, XDR, and BNF or ABNF.
sections.plainLanguage: XML is readable and can be extended, but it can use more space and processing than other formats. Protocol designers should compare those costs with the needs of their protocol.

sections.title: Well-Formed XML and Declarations
sections.content:
A protocol specification using XML should require well-formed XML. A receiver must not try to interpret part of an XML element that is not well-formed; a protocol may instead retry or abort the session.

Designers should generally avoid restrictions that exclude otherwise valid XML forms, because they can prevent use of ordinary conforming parsers. XML declarations should generally be present and must be allowed. They should be required when an encoding other than UTF-8 or UTF-16 is used.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver should reject XML that breaks XML's syntax rules rather than guess what it means. Protocol rules should also avoid unnecessary restrictions that make standard XML tools unusable.

sections.title: Validity, Meaning and Namespaces
sections.content:
Protocol designers should choose a suitable formal method for describing valid XML, such as a document type definition or XML Schema. They should explain how extensions are recognized or ignored, and what happens when data is invalid. A schema defines structure, but the protocol specification must also describe what the XML means.

Namespaces distinguish names from different vocabularies and support extensions. Specifications should reuse suitable existing namespaces and identify new ones with persistent URIs. Element and attribute choices should be consistent, and designers should plan how enumerated values can grow.
sections.plainLanguage: A schema can check the shape of XML, but it cannot explain what the data means. Protocols should define both the meaning of their data and how receivers handle extensions they do not recognize.

sections.title: Binary Data, Text and Internationalization
sections.content:
XML carries characters, not raw binary data. Binary content must be encoded, for example with Base64 or hexadecimal, or sent separately and referenced. Designers should specify how applications handle white space, since XML processors expose it to applications, and should avoid making a message's meaning depend on external resources.

XML processors support UTF-8 and UTF-16. IETF protocols using XML must allow UTF-8; allowing UTF-16 is recommended. A protocol that carries human-language text should require xml:lang when the language may affect how the text is used.
sections.plainLanguage: XML stores text, so binary data needs an encoding that turns it into characters. Protocols must allow UTF-8 and should state how language and white space affect the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XML has no built-in security services. Other protocol layers or XML-related mechanisms may provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication, and protocol specifications must require the services needed for their threats.

XML parsers process network input and must handle malformed data robustly. Implementations must not automatically access arbitrary external references supplied by untrusted sources, because doing so can cause unwanted access to external resources.
sections.plainLanguage: XML does not encrypt or authenticate data by itself. Implementations must carefully process untrusted XML and avoid automatically retrieving resources it names.
